questions.question: A 17-year-old boy training intensively for a ballet audition has had 2 weeks of worsening right buttock pain. He has been practicing turn-out, actively holding the lower limb in lateral rotation, for hours each day. He reports a deep ache in the right buttock when sitting. On examination, passive medial rotation of the right hip is restricted and painful, while hip flexion and knee strength are normal. Overuse spasm of which muscle best explains these findings?

explanations.A: Gluteus medius is chiefly a hip abductor and medial rotator, so spasm of it would not specifically limit medial rotation after lateral-rotation overuse.
explanations.B: Obturator externus lies on the external surface of the obturator membrane and is not the deep buttock muscle classically strained by turn-out in this presentation.
explanations.C: The piriformis, which runs from the anterior sacrum through the greater sciatic foramen to the greater trochanter, laterally rotates the hip; spasm causes a deep buttock ache and resists passive stretch into medial rotation.
explanations.D: Quadratus femoris is a small lateral rotator near the ischial tuberosity, but the classic overuse syndrome with deep buttock ache on sitting is piriformis syndrome.
explanations.E: Tensor fasciae latae is an anterolateral hip flexor and medial rotator, so its spasm would cause lateral hip pain rather than deep buttock pain.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, reports several months of urine leakage when she coughs, laughs, or lifts her toddler. She has no dysuria, urgency, or nocturia, and urinalysis is normal. Pelvic examination shows a weak voluntary squeeze around the examiner's fingers. Her physician recommends exercises in which she contracts as if elevating the anus or stopping the flow of urine. Weakness of which muscle group most likely underlies her symptoms?

explanations.A: Bulbospongiosus covers the vestibular bulbs and does not form the pelvic floor sling that supports the viscera and maintains continence.
explanations.B: Detrusor overactivity produces urge incontinence with urgency and frequency, not leakage triggered by raised abdominal pressure.
explanations.C: Ischiocavernosus covers the crura of the clitoris and is not a major support of the pelvic viscera.
explanations.D: The levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) supports the pelvic viscera and contracts during coughing and lifting; childbirth weakens it, causing stress incontinence that Kegel exercises can reverse.
explanations.E: The superficial transverse perineal muscles stabilize the perineal body but are not the main muscular sling for urinary continence.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man falls astride a steel beam. He has blood at the urethral meatus and cannot void. Over the next several hours he develops swelling and ecchymosis of the scrotum and penis that extends onto the lower anterior abdominal wall but stops at the upper thighs. Vital signs are stable. Extravasated urine and blood are most likely collecting in which space?

explanations.A: Rupture of the intermediate (membranous) urethra leaks into the deep pouch and pelvis, which would not track into the scrotum and abdominal wall.
explanations.B: The ischioanal fossa is a fat-filled space in the anal triangle and does not communicate with the scrotum or anterior abdominal wall.
explanations.C: The rectovesical pouch is a peritoneal recess, so fluid there would cause intraperitoneal signs rather than scrotal swelling.
explanations.D: The retropubic space fills after injury above the perineal membrane, such as bladder neck or prostatic injury, not after a straddle injury to the spongy urethra.
explanations.E: Rupture of the spongy urethra lets urine into the superficial perineal pouch beneath Colles fascia, which is continuous with Dartos and Scarpa fascia, so fluid spreads into the scrotum and up the abdominal wall but not into the thigh.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle crash with an unstable pelvic ring fracture. He has blood at the urethral meatus and a high-riding prostate on rectal examination. Retrograde urethrogram shows contrast leaking into the deep perineal pouch and pelvis just above the perineal membrane; there is no scrotal or penile swelling. Which segment of the urethra is most likely torn?
table: Contrast in deep perineal pouch and pelvis

explanations.A: The intramural (preprostatic) urethra lies within the bladder neck, so its injury would leak into the bladder region rather than the deep perineal pouch.
explanations.B: The intermediate (membranous) urethra passes through the deep perineal pouch, so its rupture leaks urine into the deep pouch and pelvic cavity above the perineal membrane.
explanations.C: The navicular fossa is the dilated distal spongy urethra within the glans, so injury there would not leak into the deep pouch.
explanations.D: The prostatic urethra is enclosed within the prostate, so injury would extravasate into the retropubic region rather than the deep perineal pouch.
explanations.E: Spongy urethral rupture leaks below the perineal membrane into the superficial pouch, producing scrotal and penile swelling, which is absent here.

questions.question: A 28-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks' gestation undergoes clinical pelvimetry. With the examiner's middle finger on the sacral promontory, the distance to the inferior margin of the pubic symphysis is measured. The obstetrician uses this value to estimate the narrowest fixed diameter that the fetal head must pass through, a diameter that does not change with pregnancy hormones. Which diameter is being estimated?

explanations.A: The anatomical conjugate runs to the superior margin of the pubic symphysis and is not the narrowest fixed passage for the fetal head.
explanations.B: The interspinous diameter is measured between the ischial spines, not along the sacral promontory–symphysis axis.
explanations.C: The oblique diameter crosses the inlet from the sacroiliac joint to the opposite iliopubic eminence and is not estimated from the diagonal conjugate.
explanations.D: The true obstetric conjugate, from the sacral promontory to the posterosuperior pubic symphysis, is the narrowest fixed distance the head must pass and is estimated from the diagonal conjugate, the only diameter measurable on exam.
explanations.E: The transverse diameter spans the widest part of the pelvic inlet and cannot be measured on bimanual exam.

questions.question: A forensic anthropologist examines a skeletal pelvis. The subpubic angle formed by the ischiopubic rami measures 85°, the greater pelvis is shallow, the ilium is thin, the obturator foramen is oval, and the acetabulum is small. These features reflect estrogen-driven development. Which additional feature would this pelvis most likely show?

explanations.A: A deeper greater pelvis is a testosterone-driven feature, the opposite of the shallow greater pelvis already described.
explanations.B: A heart-shaped inlet is typical of testosterone-driven pelvic development rather than estrogen-driven development.
explanations.C: A larger acetabulum is testosterone-driven; estrogen-driven pelves have a small acetabulum.
explanations.D: Estrogen-driven pelves have a larger greater sciatic notch, not a narrower one.
explanations.E: Estrogen-driven development produces a rounder pelvic inlet, along with a wider outlet, a pubic angle over 80°, and less sacral curvature.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman has 3 days of severe vulvar pain that worsens with sitting and walking. Examination shows a tender, fluctuant 4-cm mass in the posterolateral vaginal vestibule at the 5 o'clock position, deep to the bulb of the vestibule. The gland involved normally lies alongside the bulbospongiosus muscle. In which anatomical space is this gland located?

explanations.A: The deep perineal pouch contains the external urethral sphincter and deep transverse perineal muscles, not the greater vestibular glands.
explanations.B: The ischioanal fossa is a fat-filled space of the anal triangle; an abscess there would present perianally, not in the vestibule.
explanations.C: The rectouterine pouch is a peritoneal recess above the pelvic floor, far from the vestibule.
explanations.D: The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands lie in the superficial perineal pouch beside the bulbs of the vestibule, and infection (Bartholinitis) can swell them to 4–5 cm.
explanations.E: The vesicouterine pouch is a peritoneal recess between bladder and uterus, unrelated to vestibular glands.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman in the second stage of labor requests regional analgesia of the perineum. The anesthesiologist inserts a needle transvaginally toward a palpable bony projection on the lateral pelvic wall and injects local anesthetic just medial to the sacrospinous ligament. Which bony landmark guides this nerve block?

explanations.A: The anterior superior iliac spine is an abdominal wall landmark used near the ilioinguinal nerve, not the pudendal nerve.
explanations.B: The pudendal nerve crosses the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, so the ischial spine is the transvaginal landmark for a pudendal block.
explanations.C: The ischial tuberosity is palpated externally and marks the lateral perineal angle, not the point where the pudendal nerve crosses.
explanations.D: The pubic tubercle is an anterior landmark for inguinal structures and is not near the pudendal nerve.
explanations.E: The sacral promontory is the landmark for the diagonal conjugate, not for nerve blocks.

questions.question: A surgeon dissecting the gluteal region traces a nerve that leaves the pelvis inferior to the piriformis, curves around the sacrospinous ligament, and then passes forward to supply the external anal sphincter and perineal muscles. Through which opening does this nerve enter the perineum?

explanations.A: The greater sciatic foramen is where the nerve leaves the pelvis for the gluteal region, not where it enters the perineum.
explanations.B: The pudendal nerve and vessels enter the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen, which links the gluteal region and pelvis with the perineum.
explanations.C: The obturator canal carries the obturator nerve and vessels to the medial thigh.
explanations.D: The superficial inguinal ring transmits the spermatic cord or round ligament and the ilioinguinal nerve, not the pudendal nerve.
explanations.E: The urogenital hiatus is the gap in the levator ani for the urethra and vagina and does not transmit the pudendal nerve.

questions.question: A 78-year-old thin woman has intermittent pain along the medial thigh and knee that worsens with coughing. CT shows a loop of small bowel herniating through a canal in the superior part of the obturator foramen. On examination she has weakness of one movement of the ipsilateral thigh. Which movement is most likely weak?

explanations.A: Thigh abduction is performed by the gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve through the greater sciatic foramen.
explanations.B: The obturator canal carries the obturator nerve to the medial thigh muscles, so compression there weakens thigh adduction.
explanations.C: Dorsiflexion depends on the deep fibular nerve, a sciatic branch that does not pass through the obturator canal.
explanations.D: Knee extension is performed by the quadriceps, supplied by the femoral nerve, which does not pass through the obturator canal.
explanations.E: Plantar flexion depends on the tibial nerve, a sciatic branch that exits through the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman has new fecal incontinence 6 months after a prolonged vaginal delivery with forceps. Defecography shows loss of the normal anterior angulation at the anorectal junction during rest and squeeze. Injury to which muscle best explains the loss of this angle?

explanations.A: The coccygeus runs from the ischial spine to the coccyx and does not sling around the anorectal junction.
explanations.B: The iliococcygeus forms the posterolateral levator plate but does not create the anorectal angle.
explanations.C: The internal anal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle that maintains resting tone but does not create the anorectal angle.
explanations.D: The obturator internus is a pelvic wall muscle and lateral rotator of the hip, and does not support the anorectal junction.
explanations.E: Contraction of the puborectalis pulls the anorectal junction anteriorly to form the angle that maintains fecal continence, and it is one of the levator ani muscles most often injured in childbirth.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has a fluctuant, tender swelling lateral to the anus. CT shows a fat-containing space bounded laterally by the obturator internus and its fascia and medially by the external anal sphincter, filled with an abscess. Which neurovascular structure, running in the lateral wall of this space, is at risk during surgical drainage?

explanations.A: The inferior gluteal artery exits through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis to supply the gluteus maximus, not the ischioanal fossa wall.
explanations.B: The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal toward the medial thigh, away from the anal triangle.
explanations.C: The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels run in the pudendal canal within the obturator fascia on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.
explanations.D: The sciatic nerve runs in the gluteal region and posterior thigh, outside the ischioanal fossa.
explanations.E: The superior gluteal nerve exits above the piriformis to supply the gluteus medius and minimus, far from the anal triangle.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man notices bright red blood coating his stool and on the toilet paper for 2 weeks. He has no anal pain, and external inspection of the anus is normal. Anoscopy shows engorged vascular cushions proximal to the pectinate line. Which condition is most likely?

explanations.A: An anal fissure is a tear below the pectinate line and causes severe pain with defecation.
explanations.B: External hemorrhoids are clots in the external rectal plexus below the pectinate line and are very painful.
explanations.C: Internal hemorrhoids lie above the pectinate line, where there is no somatic pain sensation, so they cause painless bright red bleeding.
explanations.D: An ischioanal abscess presents with a painful, fluctuant swelling and fever rather than painless bleeding.
explanations.E: A perianal fistula presents with persistent purulent drainage from an external opening, usually after an abscess.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman with chronic constipation develops sudden, exquisitely painful swelling at the anal verge after straining. Examination shows a tense, bluish 1-cm nodule covered by skin, distal to the pectinate line. Thrombosis within which venous structure is most likely responsible?

explanations.A: External hemorrhoids are clots in the external rectal plexus, caused by impaired venous return from constipation or high intra-abdominal pressure, and are very painful because they lie below the pectinate line.
explanations.B: The internal pudendal vein drains the perineum through the pudendal canal and is not the site of a perianal clot.
explanations.C: The internal rectal plexus lies above the pectinate line and forms internal hemorrhoids, which are painless.
explanations.D: The middle rectal vein drains the lower rectum into the internal iliac vein and does not form a skin-covered perianal nodule.
explanations.E: The superior rectal vein drains the internal rectal plexus to the portal system, and its dilation causes internal, not external, hemorrhoids.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man has had difficulty maintaining penile rigidity since a perineal crush injury damaged the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2–S4). Further testing shows impaired contraction of a muscle that covers each crus of the penis and normally compresses the deep dorsal vein, forcing blood into the distal penis. Which muscle is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Bulbospongiosus covers the bulb of the penis and mainly expels the last drops of urine and semen.
explanations.B: The cremaster derives from the internal oblique and retracts the testis, with no role in erection.
explanations.C: The deep transverse perineal muscle lies in the deep pouch and stabilizes the perineal body.
explanations.D: The external urethral sphincter in the deep pouch controls voluntary urine flow, not erection.
explanations.E: The ischiocavernosus covers the crura and, supplied by the perineal nerve, compresses the deep dorsal vein to force blood distally and maintain erection.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man reports dribbling a few drops of urine into his clothing shortly after he finishes voiding. Uroflowmetry is normal and post-void residual volume is minimal. His urologist explains that a perineal muscle surrounding the bulb of the penis normally contracts at the end of micturition to empty the spongy urethra. Which muscle is described?

explanations.A: Bulbospongiosus, innervated by the perineal nerve (S2–S4), surrounds the bulb of the penis and contracts to expel the last drops of urine and semen.
explanations.B: The detrusor empties the bladder; a normal post-void residual shows it is working, and it does not clear the spongy urethra.
explanations.C: Ischiocavernosus covers the crura and maintains erection rather than emptying the urethra.
explanations.D: The levator ani supports the pelvic viscera and maintains continence but does not surround the penile bulb.
explanations.E: The superficial transverse perineal muscles stabilize the perineal body and do not compress the urethra.

questions.question: During open repair of an indirect inguinal hernia in a 30-year-old man, the surgeon opens the coverings of the spermatic cord from superficial to deep. The innermost fascial layer, just external to the ductus deferens and testicular vessels, is continuous with the deep inguinal ring. From which abdominal wall layer is this covering derived?

explanations.A: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the outermost covering, the external spermatic fascia.
explanations.B: The internal oblique gives rise to the middle layer, the cremasteric muscle and fascia.
explanations.C: Parietal peritoneum forms the tunica vaginalis around the testis, not a cord fascial layer.
explanations.D: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost cord covering, derives from the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring.
explanations.E: The transversus abdominis does not contribute a layer to the spermatic cord.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy is examined for an apparently undescended testis. When the examiner strokes his upper medial thigh, the ipsilateral testis briskly retracts toward the inguinal canal and later descends again into the scrotum. The muscle responsible for this retraction is derived from which abdominal wall layer?

explanations.A: The external oblique aponeurosis gives rise to the external spermatic fascia, which contains no muscle.
explanations.B: The cremaster muscle, which retracts the testis, derives from the internal oblique muscle along with the cremasteric fascia.
explanations.C: Parietal peritoneum forms the tunica vaginalis, a serous sac with no contractile fibers.
explanations.D: Transversalis fascia forms the internal spermatic fascia, which has no muscle fibers.
explanations.E: The transversus abdominis does not extend into the spermatic cord coverings.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman has a sensation of vaginal bulging 1 year after a vaginal delivery in which a midline episiotomy extended posteriorly. Examination shows a thinned, attenuated region midway between the ischial tuberosities, at the point where the bulbospongiosus, superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, and the external anal sphincter normally converge. Disruption of which structure most likely accounts for her loss of pelvic support?

explanations.A: The anococcygeal ligament lies posterior to the anus, behind the anal triangle, not midway between the ischial tuberosities.
explanations.B: The perineal body is the fibromuscular confluence at the center of the perineum where membranes and sphincters converge; stretching or episiotomy weakens it and predisposes to prolapse.
explanations.C: The perineal membrane spans the ischiopubic rami across the urogenital triangle and is not the central point where these muscles converge.
explanations.D: The sacrospinous ligament runs from the ischial spine to the sacrum and forms part of the sciatic foramina, not the central perineum.
explanations.E: The tendinous arch is the fascial origin of the levator ani on the pelvic sidewall, not a central perineal structure.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man has deep pain in the posterior hip after a fall. MRI shows a tendon that leaves the pelvis by turning sharply around the lesser sciatic notch, passing through the lesser sciatic foramen to insert on the posterior greater trochanter. The muscle arises inside the pelvis from the ilium, ischium, and obturator membrane and is supplied by L5–S2. Which muscle is described?

explanations.A: The gluteus minimus arises from the external ilium and inserts on the anterior greater trochanter without passing through a sciatic foramen.
explanations.B: The obturator externus arises from the external surface of the obturator membrane and does not pass through the lesser sciatic foramen.
explanations.C: The obturator internus arises within the pelvis, exits through the lesser sciatic foramen to the greater trochanter, is supplied by L5–S2, and laterally rotates the thigh.
explanations.D: The piriformis arises from the anterior sacrum and exits through the greater sciatic foramen, supplied by S1–S2.
explanations.E: The quadratus femoris arises from the ischial tuberosity outside the pelvis and does not pass through a foramen.
